University of Minnesota, Morris and Michigan Tech University were once part of the NSIC family as well.|access-date=2016-08-25}}{{cite book |url=https://www.revisor.mn.gov/laws/1858/0/General+Laws/Chapter/79/pdf/ |title=Minnesota Laws First Legislature: An Act to Provide for the Establishment of State Normal Schools |date=August 2, 1858 |publisher=Minnesota State Legislative Reference Library |location=Saint Paul |pages=261–264 |access-date=7 August 2018}} is a [[public university]] in [[Mankato, Minnesota]], United States. It is Minnesota's second-largest university{{cite web |url=http://www.mnscu.edu/board/materials/2013/may22/fin-04-supplement.pdf |title=FY2014 Operating Budget |publisher=MnSCU |date=May 22, 2013 |access-date=August 8, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131212200220/http://www.mnscu.edu/board/materials/2013/may22/fin-04-supplement.pdf |archive-date=December 12, 2013 |url-status=dead |df=mdy-all }}{{cite web |title=Minnesota State University overtakes St. Cloud as MnSCU enrollment continues decline|publisher=Mankato Free Press |url=http://www.mankatofreepress.com/news/local_news/article_1535815e-95e3-5701-b9d0-d06bc85af8c7.html |access-date=September 11, 2014}}, and has over 145,000 living alumni worldwide. Founded in 1868, it is the second-oldest member of the [[Minnesota State Colleges and Universities system]] and is commonly referred to as the flagship institution.{{cite web |title=President Davenport responds to Free Press questions |url=https://www.mnsu.edu/news/read/?id=old-1207229736&paper=topstories |access-date=July 22, 2015 |publisher=Mankato Free Press}}{{cite web |title=Making a monetary mark: economic impact |url=http://www.stcloudstate.edu/news/scsunow/default.asp?storyID=20073 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140919191417/http://www.stcloudstate.edu/news/scsunow/default.asp?storyID=20073 |archive-date=September 19, 2014 |access-date=July 22, 2015}} It was established as the "Second State Normal School" in 1858 and officially opened as "Mankato Normal School" a decade later.{{cite web |author1=Thomas Zahn |date=December 25, 2009 |title=City of Mankato Historical Context Study: Mankato's University |url=https://www.mankatomn.gov/home/showdocument?id=7327 |access-date=7 August 2018 |website=City of Mankato |publisher=Mankato Heritage Preservation Commission}}{{cite book |url=https://www.revisor.mn.gov/laws/1867/0/Special+Laws/Chapter/61/pdf/ |title=Minnesota State Laws 9th Legislature: An Act authorising the trustees of the village of Mankato to issue bonds for the purpose of aiding in the establishment of the Second State Normal School |date=February 16, 1867 |publisher=Minnesota State Legislative Library |pages=243–244 |access-date=7 August 2018}} Across seven colleges and schools, Minnesota State offers over 130 undergraduate programs of study, over 80 master's programs, and 4 doctoral programs.{{cite web |title=The Basic Stuff Student Handbook |url=http://www.mnsu.edu/welcome3/Publications/basic-stuff/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20000817190827/http://www.mnsu.edu/welcome3/Publications/basic-stuff/ |archive-date=August 17, 2000 |access-date=August 25, 2016 |publisher=Minnesota State University, Mankato}} MNSU has two satellite campuses: one in the Twin Cities suburb [[Edina, Minnesota|Edina]] and one in [[Owatonna, Minnesota|Owatonna]]. Through the College of Extended Learning, it provides bachelor's degrees online and at the [[Normandale Community College|Normandale Partnership Center]] in [[Bloomington, Minnesota|Bloomington]]. In 2023, MNSU partnered with [[Saint Paul College]] to launch the Minnesota Polytechnic and Applied Learning Institute (MinnPoly), becoming Minnesota's first [[Institute of technology|polytechnic institute]].{{Cite web |title=MinnPoly Institute Takes New Approach to Higher Education |url=https://www.saintpaul.edu:443/news/minnpoly-institute-takes-new-approach-to-higher-education |access-date=2023-02-11 |website=www.saintpaul.edu |language=en-US}}{{Cite web |last=McShane |first=Michael |title=MSU Mankato's MinnPoly Institute takes new approach to higher education |url=https://www.keyc.com/2023/01/10/msu-mankatos-minnpoly-institute-takes-new-approach-higher-education/ |access-date=2023-02-11 |website=www.keyc.com |language=en}} The [[Minnesota State Mavericks]] compete in 21 intercollegiate sports, most at the [[NCAA Division II]] level in the [[Northern Sun Intercollegiate Conference]]. Its men's and women's ice hockey teams compete at the [[NCAA Division I|Division I]] level, respectively in the [[Central Collegiate Hockey Association]] (CCHA) and [[Western Collegiate Hockey Association]] (WCHA). ==History== === 1860–1921: Founding and early years === [[File:Old Main at Mankato State Normal School, Mankato, Minnesota - DPLA - 81f70c182ca26315cecdaf6fa013a9a1.jpg|alt=Image of Old Main at Mankato State Normal School, Mankato, Minnesota before fire of 1922.|thumb|left|Old Main at Mankato Normal School, Mankato, Minnesota]] The state legislature recognized the need for an education center in southern Minnesota in 1858.{{cite web |url=https://npgallery.nps.gov/nrhp/AssetDetail?assetID=d81bd682-b618-4f20-bbb9-f4cc1344f5d2|title=Old Main and the Annex, Mankato State Teachers College |author=Rosie, Charlene |date=December 1, 1982|publisher=United States National Park Service |access-date=August 5, 2016}} In 1860, the legislature chartered the development of state-run normal schools across the state. The largest and fastest-growing cities outside of Saint Paul, Saint Cloud and Mankato, were selected for the sites, dependent on local fundraising to establish the schools with seed money. Through the efforts of local attorney and state legislator Daniel Buck, the newly formed [[Mankato, Minnesota|City of Mankato]] donated $5,000 raised from the community and sold $5,000 in bonds to found the second state [[normal school]], Mankato Normal School.{{cite web|title=A Look at Minnesota State University's History |publisher=Minnesota State University, Mankato |url=http://www.mnsu.edu/about/history.html |access-date=January 25, 2015}} It was chartered in state law in 1860 and held its first classes in 1868, with an enrollment of 27.{{r|MSU150Years|p=4}} The school's original mission was to train and educate teachers for rural schools in southern Minnesota. Early coursework included mathematics, science, civil engineering, agriculture, western classics, and basic pedagogy. The first Normal School-owned building's [[cornerstone]] was laid on June 22, 1869.{{r|MSU150Years|p=4}} George M. Gage served as Mankato Normal School's principal from 1868 to 1872.{{r|MSU150Years|p=6}} [[File:Portrait of Principal Julia Ann Sears, Mankato, Minnesota - DPLA - 4a858c81f4b49e2b9fb9c6a3c465bcc9.jpg|alt=Portrait of Julia Ann Sears|thumb|242x242px|Portrait of [[Julia Sears]]]] During this period, Mankato Normal School provided educational certificates that allowed graduates to become schoolteachers, and most of the students were women.{{cite web|title=Historical Sketch of Minnesota State University, Mankato|publisher=William E. Lass|url=http://sbs.mnsu.edu/history/ngphc/msu_history.php|access-date=January 25, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150206072238/http://sbs.mnsu.edu/history/ngphc/msu_history.php|archive-date=February 6, 2015|url-status=dead|df=mdy-all}} In relation to this focus on women's education, Mankato Normal School is noted as the first public college in the U.S. to be headed by a woman, suffragette [[Julia Sears]], in 1872. In 1873, the State Normal Board demoted Sears to assistant principal, replacing her as principal with David C. John.{{r|MSU150Years|p=8}} Sears's salary as assistant principal was reduced from $1,500 to $1,200 and resulted in a letter to Gage that it was doubtful that she would see him again in Minnesota.{{r|MSU150Years|p=8}}{{r|Julia A. Sears}} In response, the assistant principal position was offered to Cornelius Hyde.{{r|MSU150Years|p=8}} Both Sears and Hyde arrived for work on September 1, 1873.{{r|Julia A. Sears}} After it was determined that Hyde would receive the position, 41 students refused to attend classes and 32 were expelled for failing to return after three days.{{r|Julia A. Sears}} 60 residents signed a petition requesting that Hyde return to his position as instructor and that Sears be reinstated as assistant principal.{{r|MSU150Years|p=8}}{{r|Julia A. Sears}} This became known as the "Sears Rebellion",{{r|Julia A. Sears}} which lasted until Sears left the school for a professorship at [[Peabody Normal School]]. These events were commemorated when a new residence hall was dedicated in honor of Sears in 2008 and a commission on the status of women was founded to support the advancement of women's education at the institution in the 1990s. === 1921–1957: Teaching college, post-WWII expansion === [[File:Old Main and Annex.jpg|thumb|[[Old Main (Minnesota State University, Mankato)|Old Main]] of the historic lower campus. Built in 1924, it now hosts a senior living community]] By 1921, the school had grown to the point that it began to offer four-year bachelor's degrees. As a result, it was renamed "Mankato State Teachers College". The original [[Old Main]] building was destroyed in a fire in 1922 and a new building was completed on April 4, 1924.{{r|MSU150Years|pp=21,26}} Enrollment dipped during [[World War II]] and the college refocused its extension programs on providing education to members of the [[Works Progress Administration]] and Naval Corps. Clarence L. Crawford became college president in 1946. He held the position for 20 years, overseeing and promoting tremendous growth of the college from approximately 400 students at the time of his arrival to about 14,000 when he retired in 1966. During the postwar period, student enrollment expanded greatly. The original university buildings were then in what was known as the Valley Campus, down the hill in lower Mankato. The Valley Campus's size and footprint lacked the space needed to handle the growing student body. The Mankato Teachers College received 12 former Army [[barracks]] as a short-term solution.{{r|MSU150Years|p=40}} By the late 1950s work began on an entirely new, modern campus atop the river valley bluff. This became the Highland Campus. An experimental school, the Wilson School, was built on the Highland Campus to research and apply new teaching methods for students in grades K–12. The intention was to provide student teachers the opportunity to learn and experiment with new methods in a university environment.{{cite web|title=Wilson Campus School Collection, 1917-2002 |url=https://lib.mnsu.edu/archives/fa/msu/msu307.html|website=Minnesota State University, Mankato, University Archives |publisher=Southern Minnesota Historical Center|access-date=April 13, 2018}} === 1957–1995: Transition to comprehensive university === [[File:Old Main on fire at Mankato Teacher's College, Mankato, Minnesota - DPLA - 8d916c2ff6cfe47a3609edbf77a10b32.jpg|alt=image of Old Main on fire at Mankato Teacher's College, Mankato, Minnesota|thumb|Old Main on fire at Mankato State Teachers College, Mankato, Minnesota]] By 1957, the institution's mission had broadened to comprehensive four-year college education, and the legislature changed the school's name to Mankato State College. By the 1960s the institution had grown so rapidly that a bill was proposed in the state legislature to elevate it to university status. Originally, Mankato State was to have been renamed the University of Southern Minnesota; a later amendment would have renamed it Minnesota State University.{{cite news |last1=Star Statehouse Burea |title=Senate Gets Mankato 'U'Bill |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/188217591 |access-date=June 7, 2018 |agency=Newspaper.com |publisher=The Minneapolis Star |date=April 19, 1963 |location=Minneapolis, Minnesota |page=30 |quote=Bills to give Mankato State College university status, to create a new college in southwestern Minnesota and set up a state-run system of junior colleges were sent to the floor of the Minnesota Senate today. All three bills won approval by the Senate Finance Committee Thursday. Mankato would be called 'Minnesota State University' rather than the University of Southern Minnesota, according to an amendment approved last night as proposed by Senator Michael McGuire of Montgomery, Minnesota (Liberal party).}} (These were proposed long before the television show ''[[Coach (TV series)|Coach]]'' aired.{{cite news|title=Mankato College May be 'Minnesota State'|url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/84147230|access-date=July 24, 2017|agency=Associated Press|publisher=La Crosse Tribune|date=April 19, 1963}}) It was to be a second and independent state university equal in stature to the [[University of Minnesota]] at a time when there was only one research institution.{{cite book|last1=Youel|first1=Donald|title=Mankato State College: An Interpretative Essay|date=January 1, 1968|publisher=Minnesota State University, Mankato|location=Mankato, Minnesota|pages=60–61|edition=4}} There was significant opposition from the University of Minnesota and from Governor [[Karl Rolvaag]] at the time. [[File:Bell Tower MNSU.jpg|thumb|180px|The Ostrander-Student Memorial Bell Tower stands in the campus arboretum. It was completed in 1989]] In 1975 the college successfully made the case for university status and was renamed "Mankato State University". This change reflected a further 40% growth in the student body to 12,000 students by 1972. Following this, the number of programs increased, to include science, technology, engineering, health sciences, and others. While the transition to "state university" was being considered, the administration also explored the prospect of combining the Valley Campus buildings with the Highland Campus on the recommendation of a consultant hired by the Higher Education Coordinating Commission.{{r|MSU150Years|p=60}} Despite some faculty opposition to the merger, Mankato State University received permission to consolidate in May 1977 and completed the consolidation under President Margaret Preska on May 5, 1980.{{r|MSU150Years|p=60}} The Valley Campus was eventually sold to a private developer and the Highland Campus grew. === 1995–present: Minnesota State system, doctoral offerings === In 1995, the seven state universities were transferred to the newly created [[Minnesota State Colleges and Universities system]] by a mandate from the state legislature. The university was renamed Minnesota State University, Mankato in 1998 in recognition of its significant contribution to the state's higher education system.{{cite web|title=History and Tradition |publisher=Minnesota State University, Mankato |url=http://www.mnsu.edu/students/basicstuff/history.html|access-date=January 25, 2015}} This name change was also intended to broaden recognition of the university in the Midwest.{{cite web|url=http://www.mnscu.edu/media/newsreleases/1998/September18.html|author=Doug Anderson|title=MnSCU Board Approves Mankato State University Name Change|access-date=August 5, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160821075917/http://www.mnscu.edu/media/newsreleases/1998/September18.html|archive-date=August 21, 2016|url-status=dead|df=mdy-all}} Richard Rush, then the president of the university, said of the name change, "Our goal is to make this university the other great public university in Minnesota."{{cite news |title=Mankato State University to Change Name to Minnesota State University, Mankato|url=http://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/mankato-state-university-to-change-name-to-minnesota-state-university-mankato-76648697.html|access-date=October 9, 2016 |agency=PRnewsWire|publisher=Mankato State University|date=September 18, 1998}} This marked a significant change in direction in the institution's history, one that would later be realized as it fought to be authorized to award doctoral degrees. It was during this time that the institution began to call itself '''Minnesota State'''. In 2007, in another major milestone, the university was authorized to begin offering applied doctoral degrees.{{cite web |title=Minnesota State Mankato to confer first doctoral degrees|publisher=Minnesota State University, Mankato |url=http://www.mnsu.edu/news/read/?id=old-1241538734&paper=topstories |access-date=January 25, 2015}} ==Academics== {{Infobox US university ranking | USNWR_REG = 75 | Wamo_MASTERSU = 250 | Forbes = 344 }} MNSU offers over 130 undergraduate programs of study, 13 pre-professional programs, and over 85 graduate programs. It provides a comprehensive education: each undergraduate program of study includes general requirements in mathematics, writing, cultural diversity, speech, information technology, and the environment. Minnesota State is among the nation's top-producing master's institutions of [[Fulbright Program|Fulbright]] recipients, producing 11 student grant awards and 41 Fulbright Scholars.{{cite web|title=Top Producers of U.S. Fulbright Scholars by Type of Institution, 2010–11|url=http://chronicle.com/article/Table-Top-Producers-of-US/125072/|publisher=The Chronicle of Higher Education|access-date=February 5, 2015}}{{Cite web |title=Minnesota State University, Mankato {{!}} Fulbright Scholar Program |url=https://fulbrightscholars.org/institution/minnesota-state-university-mankato |access-date=2023-02-25 |website=fulbrightscholars.org}}{{Cite web |title=Grantee Directory |url=https://us.fulbrightonline.org/alumni/grantee-directory?name=&us_institution%5B%5D=6810&sort= |access-date=2023-02-25 |website=us.fulbrightonline.org}} Each year, over 3,000 students graduate from MNSU. The Office of the Registrar confers around 3,000 bachelor's, 600 master's, 50 specialist, and 10 doctoral degrees.{{cite web|title=Dec. 13: Commencement Ceremonies|publisher=Minnesota State University, Mankato|url=http://www.mnsu.edu/news/read/?id=old-1418139037&paper=topstories |access-date=January 25, 2015}} MNSU's Career Development Center reports that 85% of graduates find employment in an area related to their field, and 90% were employed or continuing their education within 12 months of graduation.{{cite web|title=Graduate Facts for 2012–2013 Graduates|publisher=Minnesota State University, Mankato |url=http://www.mnsu.edu/cdc/resources/statistics/2012-2013/index.html|access-date=January 25, 2015}}{{cite web |title=Graduate Facts for 2012–2013 Graduates|publisher=Minnesota State University, Mankato |url=http://www.mnsu.edu/cdc/resources/statistics/2012-2013/GFUinfographic.png|access-date=January 25, 2015}}{{dead link|date=February 2018 |bot=InternetArchiveBot|fix-attempted=yes}} === Organization and administration === The university is organized into seven discipline-specific colleges. Nursing Home – Minnesota State University, Mankato|author=College of Allied Health and Nursing|publisher=Minnesota State University, Mankato}} *College of Business{{cite web|url=http://cob.mnsu.edu/|title=College of Business|publisher=Minnesota State University, Mankato}} *College of Education{{cite web|url=http://ed.mnsu.edu/|title=College of Education|publisher=Minnesota State University, Mankato}} *College of Humanities & Social Sciences{{cite web|url=http://www.mnsu.edu/carts/|title=College of Arts & Humanities|author=College of Arts|publisher=Minnesota State University, Mankato}} *College of Science, Engineering and Technology{{cite web|url=http://cset.mnsu.edu/|title=Welcome to CSET – Minnesota State University, Mankato|publisher=Minnesota State University, Mankato}} *College of Graduate Studies and Research{{cite web|url=http://grad.mnsu.edu/|title=College of Graduate Studies |publisher=Minnesota State University, Mankato}} *College of Extended Learning{{cite web|url=http://www.mnsu.edu/ext/|title=University Extended Education|author=College of Extended Learning|publisher=Minnesota State University, |url=https://grad.mnsu.edu/research/research_centers.html |access-date=18 July 2018 |website=College of Graduate Studies and Research |publisher=Minnesota State University, Mankato}} {{Columns-list|colwidth=30em| *The Glen Taylor Nursing Institute *The Center on Aging *The Minnesota Center for Transportation Research and Implementation *The Center for Excellence in Scholarship and Research *The Minnesota Center for Modeling and Simulation *The Kessel Institute for Peace and Change *The Minnesota State Engineering Center of Excellence *The Minnesota Center for Rural Policy and Development *Minnesota Polytechnic and Applied Learning Institute (MinnPoly) *The School of Applied Agriculture, Food and Natural Resources *Small Business Development Center *Southern Minnesota Historical Center *The Urban and Regional Studies Institute *The Water Resources Center }} === Notable programs === MNSU has a history of creating new programs to meet the demand of new and developing fields. It was the nation's first institution to offer a Master of Fine Arts degree in [[Forensic science|forensics]].{{cite web|title=MFA-Forensics Degree Approved |publisher=Minnesota State University, Mankato Public Relations|url=http://www.mnsu.edu/news/read/?id=old-1046412000&paper=topstories |access-date=September 11, 2014}} It also offered one of the first interdisciplinary programs in [[urban studies]] and local government management.{{cite web|url=http://sbs.mnsu.edu/ursi/ |title=Urban and Regional Studies Institute – College of Social & Behavioral Sciences – Minnesota State University, Mankato|publisher=Sbs.mnsu.edu|date=October 7, 2014|access-date=July 14, 2015}} The Aviation and Airport Management program is Minnesota's only accredited aviation program.{{cite web |url=http://www.kare11.com/story/news/2015/10/27/demand-for-pilots-has-msu-mankato-program-thriving/74672922/ |title=Demand for pilots has MSU-Mankato program thriving |publisher=Kare 11 News |date=October 27, 2015 |access-date=November 16, 2015 }}{{dead link|date=April 2018 |bot=Randomeditor1000 |fix-attempted=yes }} Graduates are often hired to work in nearby states as the program also serves regional needs.{{cite web |url=http://www.mprnews.org/story/2015/10/27/aviation-msu-mankato|title=With high hopes, aviation students flock to MSU Mankato |author=Elizabeth Baier|date=October 27, 2015|publisher=Minnesota Public Radio News}}{{cite web |url=http://www.bizjournals.com/twincities/morning_roundup/2015/10/msu-mankatos-bet-on-aviation-is-paying-off.html|title=MSU Mankato's bet on aviation is paying off - Minneapolis / St. Paul Business Journal|access-date=August 8, 2016}} The university has developed national partnerships with [[Delta Air Lines]]{{cite news |last1=Painter |first1=Kristen |title=Delta begins push to attract more pilots in training |url=http://www.startribune.com/delta-begins-push-to-attract-more-people-as-pilots/488432891/ |access-date=19 October 2018 |agency=StarTribune |date=July 18, 2018}} and [[Sun Country Airlines]] that provide on-the-job training and direct hire before graduation.{{cite news |last1=Moylan |first1=Martin |title=Sun Country partners with Minnesota State Mankato for pilots |url=https://www.mprnews.org/story/2018/10/18/minnesota-state-mankato-to-supply-pilots-sun-country |access-date=19 October 2018 |agency=MPR News |publisher=Minnesota Public Radio |date=October 18, 2018}}{{cite web |last1=Van Abbema |first1=Alex |title=Sun Country Airlines partners with Minnesota State in Mankato for new pilots |url=https://www.bizjournals.com/twincities/news/2018/10/18/sun-country-airlines-partners-with-minnesota-state.html |website=Minneapolis-Saint Paul Business Journal |publisher=American City Business Journals |access-date=19 October 2018}} === Undergraduate student profile === Minnesota State's undergraduate student body includes a large proportion of residential full-time students. It attracts the second-largest number of incoming Minnesota freshmen each year.{{cite web |title=Statewide Longitudinal Data System|publisher=Minnesota Department of Education |url=http://sleds.mn.gov/#collegeActivity/orgId--999999000__groupType--state__collegeActivityCOHORTID--2013__p--7|access-date=January 26, 2015}} For 2013–2016, the institution had rolling admissions with an acceptance rate of 65.5%, and the average accepted student ACT score ranged from 20 to 25.{{cite web|title=Minnesota State University—Mankato|publisher=Us News |url=http://colleges.usnews.rankingsandreviews.com/best-colleges/minnesota-mankato-2360 |access-date=January 26, 2015}}{{cite web|title=Minnesota State University Mankato Admissions|publisher=About.com Education, Minnesota Colleges Section |url=http://collegeapps.about.com/od/collegeprofiles/p/minnesota-state-university-mankato-admissions-profile.htm |access-date=January 26, 2015}} Since the fall of 2012, the university has been the largest university in the Minnesota State system, and the second-largest in Minnesota, according to the total number of full-year equivalent students, with enrollment regularly over 15,000 students. ==Campus== {{main|Campus of Minnesota State University}} === Main campus === [[File:Minnesota State University 2.jpg|thumb|Athletic fields]] Minnesota State's main campus contains 30 buildings spread over 303 acres. The campus includes housing, academic buildings, a main library, a music library, two astronomy observatories, experimental research stations for alternative and renewable energy, a recreation center, an athletics complex, a student center, an administration center, and over 50 acres of athletics fields, including [[Blakeslee Stadium]].{{cite web|url=http://www.mnsu.edu/facilities/buildings.html |title=Buildings – Landmarks – About the University – Minnesota State University, Mankato |publisher=Minnesota State University, Mankato |access-date=August 5, 2016}} The [[Minnesota State Mavericks]] men's and women's hockey teams also use and have administrative space at the [[Mayo Clinic Health System Event Center]] and the [[All Seasons Arena (Mankato)|All Seasons Arena]] off campus. ==== Student housing ==== [[File:MSU_JuliaSears.jpg|thumb|right|393x393px|Julia Sears Residence Hall]] Minnesota State has five residence communities, housing up to 2,900 students: McElroy Hall, Crawford Hall, Preska Hall, Julia Sears Hall, and apartment-style Stadium Heights.{{Cite web |title=Room Types |url=https://www.mnsu.edu/university-life/housing/residential-life/rooms/ |access-date=2022-12-21 |website=www.mnsu.edu |language=en}} On-campus housing is optional. There are over a dozen [[Learning community|Learning Community]] programs that range from academic to hobby-based interests.{{cite web |date=December 21, 2022 |title=Learning Communities – Minnesota State University, Mankato |url=https://www.mnsu.edu/academics/academic-support/scholarly-communities/learning-communities/ |access-date=December 21, 2022 |publisher=Mnsu.edu}} === Satellite campuses === ==== Edina ==== This campus is at 7700 France Ave. S. in [[Edina, Minnesota|Edina]], and serves a diverse student body from the southwest [[Minneapolis–Saint Paul|Twin Cities metropolitan area]].{{cite web|title=Minnesota State University at Edina |url=http://www.mnsu.edu/7700france/ |access-date=January 26, 2015}} Programs at this campus include 12 undergraduate programs, including bachelor's degrees, bachelor's completion programs, undergraduate minors, and teaching licensure. The College of Graduate Studies offers 23 graduate programs, including master's degrees in accounting, engineering, education leadership, and other specialty areas. ==== Owatonna ==== The state established Owatonna College and University Center on 27 acres on [[Owatonna, Minnesota|Owatonna]]'s southwest side to meet the needs of college graduates in the Owatonna area. This site is a collaboration of Minnesota State University, Mankato, South Central College, and Riverland Community College to provide lower-division liberal arts, career, and technical education, and upper-division and graduate-level studies in one location. On average 4,000 students do for-credit coursework at this location.{{cite web|title=Three MnSCU partners collaborate in Owatonna|publisher=KEYC-TV, Mankato, MN |url=http://www.mnsu.edu/news/read/?id=old-1235062489&paper=topstories|access-date=January 26, 2015}} ==== Normandale partnership center ==== In 2012, a partnership center was established to offer several targeted bachelor's degree in the southwest Twin Cities area at [[Normandale Community College]] in [[Bloomington, Minnesota|Bloomington]].{{cite magazine |last1=Geller |first1=Steve |title=Partnership Opening Marks Beginning of New Era |url=http://www.normandale.edu/community/newsroom/publications/normandale-magazine-spring-2013/partnership-center-opening |access-date=18 July 2018 |magazine=Normandale Magazine |date=Spring 2013 |publisher=Normandale Community College}} Several trial programs originally offered at the Normandale Center, such as the Twin Cities engineering program, were expanded to other Minnesota State system community colleges in 2016.{{cite web |title=Learn engineering by doing engineering |url=https://cset.mnsu.edu/ie/tce.html |website=Twin Cities Engineering Program |publisher=College of Science, Engineering and Technology |access-date=18 July 2018}} ==Student life== {| class="wikitable floatright sortable collapsible"; text-align:right; font-size:80%;" |+ style="font-size:90%" |Undergraduate demographics as of Fall 2023{{cite web |title= College Scorecard: Minnesota State University-Mankato|url=https://collegescorecard.ed.gov/school/?173920-Minnesota-State-University-Mankato|website=College Scorecard |publisher=[[United States Department of Education]] |access-date=June 23, 2025 }} |- ! Race and ethnicity ! colspan="2" data-sort-type=number |Total |- | [[Non-Hispanic whites|White]] |align=right| {{bartable|72|%|2||background:cyan}} |- | [[International student]] |align=right| {{bartable|9|%|2||background:#008080}} |- | [[African Americans|Black]] |align=right| {{bartable|6|%|2||background:purple}} |- | [[Hispanic and Latino Americans|Hispanic]] |align=right| {{bartable|6|%|2||background:green}} |- | [[Asian Americans|Asian]] |align=right| {{bartable|3|%|2||background:orange}} |- | [[Multiracial Americans|Two or more races]] |align=right| {{bartable|3|%|2||background:violet}} |- | Unknown |align=right| {{bartable|1|%|2||background:grey}} |- ! colspan="4" data-sort-type=number |[[Economic diversity]] |- | [[American lower class|Low-income]]{{efn|The percentage of students who received an income-based federal [[Pell grant]] intended for low-income students.}} |align=right| {{bartable|24|%|2||background:red}} |- | [[Affluence in the United States|Affluent]]{{efn|The percentage of students who are a part of the [[American middle class]] at the bare minimum.}} |align=right| {{bartable|76|%|2||background:black}} |} Mankato is widely considered a [[college town]], with 32.1% of the population between the ages of 15 and 24.{{Cite web |title=Explore Census Data |url=https://data.census.gov/table?q=Mankato+city,+Minnesota&tid=ACSST5Y2021.S0101 |access-date=2023-02-26 |website=data.census.gov}} In 2017, Schools.com ranked Mankato the nation's second-best college town.{{Cite web |title=Mankato named 2nd best college town in America |url=https://www.kare11.com/article/news/education/mankato-named-2nd-best-college-town-in-america/89-464788974 |access-date=2023-02-26 |website=kare11.com |language=en-US}} === Student organizations === Students can join over 200 academic student groups, intramural sports, leadership and religious organizations, honorary and professional fraternities and sororities, and special interest groups.{{Cite web |title=Student Organizations |url=https://www.mnsu.edu/university-life/activities-and-organizations/student-organizations-leadership/rso/ |access-date=2022-12-21 |website=www.mnsu.edu |language=en}} There is an active Panhellenic Council and Intrafraternity Council. === Media === ==== Print ==== First published on March 23, 1926, ''The Reporter'' is the university's student-run newspaper.{{Cite web |last=Reporter |first=M. S. U. |date=2021-08-24 |title=The Reporter: who we are, what we stand for |url=https://www.msureporter.com/2021/08/24/the-reporter-who-we-are-what-we-stand-for/ |access-date=2022-12-21 |language=en}} It covers Minnesota State athletics and campus happenings and publishes editorials and thought pieces. Weekly editions come out during the fall and spring academic terms. Its office is in the Centennial Student Union.{{Cite web |title=Centennial Student Union Fast Facts |url=https://www.mnsu.edu/university-life/centennial-student-union/about-us/csu-fast-facts/ |access-date=2022-12-21 |website=www.mnsu.edu |language=en}} Upon its founding, the newspaper went by the name ''Among Ourselves'' and was funded by annual 50-cent subscription fees. The last issue of ''Among Ourselves'' was on April 2, 1927. The paper returned as ''School Spirit'' on March 7, 1929, and was renamed ''College Spirit'' on May 25, 1933. The last issue of ''College Spirit'' was on June 4, 1935. In fall 1936, the paper took the name ''The College Reporter'', arguing that the name "spirit" better suited a boat than a newspaper. ==== Radio ==== 89.7FM [[KMSU]] is MNSU's official radio station.{{Cite web |title=89.7 KMSU 'The Maverick' |url=https://www.mnsu.edu/kmsu-radio/ |access-date=2022-12-22 |website=www.mnsu.edu |language=en}} It was founded in 1963. === Centennial Student Union === Opened on October 27, 1967, the Centennial Student Union (CSU) is a 213,000-square-foot space that serves as a central campus hub. The CSU is home to many university departments, including Student Activities, Student Government, The Reporter, Counseling Center, Kearney International Center, Multicultural Center, Women's Center, Veterans Resource Center, LGBT Center, Maverick Bullpen, Ostrander Auditorium, and the campus bookstore. ==== Student activities ==== Student Activities at MNSU is home to a wide variety of departments, including Registered Student Organizations (RSOs), Community Engagement Office, Greek Life & Off-Campus Housing, and Student Events Team.{{Cite web |title=Student Activities |url=https://www.mnsu.edu/university-life/centennial-student-union/staff/student-activities/ |access-date=2022-12-22 |website=www.mnsu.edu |language=en}} Student Events Team hosts campus-wide events including homecoming concerts and the annual CSU Haunted House Takeover.{{Cite web |title=Student Events Team - Minnesota State Mankato |url=https://www.mnsu.edu/university-life/activities-and-organizations/student-events-team/ |access-date=2022-12-22 |website=www.mnsu.edu |language=en}} ==== LGBT center ==== MNSU is home to the nation's second-oldest LGBT resource center for students.{{cite web |last1=William|first1=Ford|title=Minnesota State University Hosts Second Oldest LGBT Center in Nation |url=http://diverseeducation.com/article/16722/|website=Inside Diverse Education|publisher=Inside Diverse Education|access-date=April 28, 2016}} Originally called the "Alternative Lifestyles Office", the center was founded by Minnesota State alumnus [[James Chalgren]] in 1977. Located in the Centennial Student Union, it is an independent office within the university's division of Student Affairs. According to ''[[The Advocate (LGBT magazine)|The Advocate]]'', Minnesota State was voted one of the nation's top 100 campuses for LGBT students.{{cite web|last1=Bradbury|first1=Kathleen|title=Higher Education|url=http://www.lavendermagazine.com/our-affairs/out-on-campus/|website=Lavender Magazine|publisher=The Advocate Periodical|access-date=April 28, 2016}} ==Athletics== {{Main|Minnesota State Mavericks}} [[File:Minnesota State Mavericks logo.png|thumb|250x250px|Logo of the [[Minnesota State Mavericks]]]] The [[Minnesota State Mavericks]] consists of eight men's and ten women's varsity teams. More than 650 students participate in athletics each year for the university. It offers teams in men's and women's hockey and basketball, football, baseball, golf, women's swimming, track, cross country, women's tennis, wrestling, soccer, golf, volleyball, and softball. The men's and women's [[ice hockey]] teams both compete in [[NCAA Division I]]—the men in the [[Central Collegiate Hockey Association]] (CCHA) and the women in the [[Western Collegiate Hockey Association]] (WCHA). The men's team had competed in the WCHA through the 2020–21 season, but was one of the seven men's WCHA members that left after that season to reestablish the CCHA, leading to the WCHA disbanding its men's division. Other university athletic teams began competing in the [[Northern Sun Intercollegiate Conference]] of [[NCAA Division II]] in 2008–09 following the disbandment of the North Central Conference. The school mascot is [[Stomper the Maverick|Stomper]] the Maverick, a caricature of a wild steer. The school colors are purple and gold, officially announced in 1892. In 1926, the M club voted to change the athletic teams' colors to burnt orange and navy blue because purple and gold were too similar to [[Winona State University]]'s colors. The orange and blue uniforms were discontinued in 1955.{{Cite book |last=Lass |first=William E. |title=Minnesota State University, Mankato 1868-2018: A Sesquicentennial History |publisher=Minnesota State University, Mankato |year=2018 |isbn=978-0-9729134-6-1 |location=Mankato, Minnesota |pages= |language=English}} [[File:MSU Mankato Men's and Women's championship teams 2024 - DSC02606 (53681152493).jpg|thumb|Championship men's and women's basketball teams meeting Gov. [[Tim Walz]] in 2024]] Minnesota State athletics teams have placed favorably in national competitions in [[NCAA Division II]] athletics in several sports including hockey, football, baseball, women's basketball, men's basketball, men's track & field, wrestling, women's soccer and softball. Since 1993, the Mavericks have captured the most individual national championships out of all sixteen colleges and universities in the [[Northern Sun Intercollegiate Conference|Northern Sun Conference]].{{cite web |url=http://northernsun.org/sports/2011/8/10/National_Championshps.aspx?path=general |title=NSIC National Championships |publisher=Northern Sun Intercollegiate Conference |date=March 11, 2015 |access-date=August 11, 2015}} The 2015 season marked the 14th straight year that the Mavericks finished in the top 25 in the country in the national standings, and the seventh time Minnesota State had posted a top-five placing for the Learfield Sports Directors' Cup.{{cite web|url=http://www.mnsu.edu/news/read/?id=1433434030&paper=topstories |title=Mavericks Athletics Ranked No. 5 Nationally in 2014–15 — Minnesota State University, Mankato (MSU) – 2015-06-04 |publisher=Mnsu.edu |access-date=July 14, 2015}}{{cite web|url=http://www.nacda.com/sports/directorscup/spec-rel/060415aaa.html |title=Final Division II & Division III Learfield Sports Directors' Cup Standings Released NACDA.COM :: NACDA Official Web Site |publisher=Nacda.com |date=June 4, 2015 |access-date=July 14, 2015}} It has also won the NSIC US Bank All-Sports Award four times and placed second twice during the last six-year period of the 2008–2015 competition seasons.{{cite web |url=http://www.msumavericks.com/news/2015/5/12/GEN_0512155538.aspx |title=Mavericks Finish Second in 2014–15 NSIC/US Bank All-Sports Standings |publisher=Minnesota State Mavericks Athletics |date=May 12, 2015 |access-date=August 11, 2015}}{{cite web |url=http://www.northernsun.org/news/2015/3/11/GEN_0311155418.aspx |title=2014–15 NSIC / US Bank Winter All-Sports Standings |publisher=Northern Sun Intercollegiate Conference |date=March 11, 2015 |access-date=August 11, 2015}} In 2024, the Mavericks won the [[2024 NCAA Division II men's basketball tournament|men's]] and [[2024 NCAA Division II women's basketball tournament|women's Division II basketball tournaments]], making them the first school in four decades to win both in the same year.{{cite news |last1=Yang |first1=Hannah |title=Mankato celebrates women's and men's NCAA Division II championship wins |url=https://www.mprnews.org/story/2024/04/01/mankato-celebrates-womens-and-mens-ncaa-division-ii-championship-wins |access-date=10 December 2024 |work=MPR News |date=April 1, 2024}} The Minnesota State fight song is "[[The Minnesota State Rouser]]", also known as the "Maverick Rouser".{{cite news |last1=Alleven|first1=Monica|title=Fight Song composer never thought it would last this long |url=https://arch.lib.mnsu.edu/islandora/object/MSUrepository:104233|access-date=November 19, 2017|publisher=Minnesota State University Reporter|date=October 23, 1986}} It is played at all the athletics events as well as other events, along with the school song, "[[The Minnesota State Hymn]]". The [[Minnesota State University Marching Band]] is called the "Maverick Machine", and drives enthusiasm and school spirit at athletics events. [[File:Taylor Center Hall.jpg|thumb|265x265px|Constructed in 2000, the Taylor Center is home to Bresnan Arena.]] Minnesota State hosted the [[Minnesota Vikings]] summer training camp from 1966 to 2017. Each year over 60,000 fans traveled to [[Blakeslee Stadium]] to watch the team practice, attend signing events and meet and greets, followed by a fireworks show.{{cite web |title=Businesses, city ready for Vikings training camp |publisher=Mankato Free Press |url=http://www.mankatofreepress.com/news/local_news/businesses-city-ready-for-vikings-training-camp/article_ac09ed39-3949-5956-90ac-947bdb811af7.html |access-date=January 25, 2015}} In 2017, the Vikings ownership announced they would move the annual tradition to [[Eagan, Minnesota]], following the construction of a new facility.{{cite web|title=Vikings Announce that this is the last training camp in Mankato|url=http://www.mankatofreepress.com/news/local_news/vikings-announce-that-this-is-last-training-camp-in-mankato/article_3ca3ff32-6bc1-11e7-abd0-8fac119011bf.html|website=Mankato Free Press|publisher=Mankato Free Press|access-date=July 21, 2017}} The Vikings have since established a scholarship for Minnesota State students. ===Facility renovations and upgrades=== The Taylor Center opened in 2000, and was made possible by the donations of alumnus [[Glen Taylor]]. The 4,800-seat facility houses Maverick basketball, volleyball and wrestling teams. The MNSU Admissions office is also there, and the 5,000 square-foot Hall of Champions showcases the university's history. In addition to [[Minnesota State Mavericks]] events, the Taylor Center hosts commencement ceremonies, concerts and lectures.{{cite web|title=Taylor Center |url=http://www.msumavericks.com/sports/2009/9/8/GEN_0908091827.aspx|website=Athletics Facilities|publisher=Minnesota State University Mavericks Athletics department|access-date=November 19, 2017}} == Notable people == {{Main|List of Minnesota State University, Mankato people}} File:Tim Walz official photo.jpg|[[Tim Walz]] (M.S., 2001) – 41st [[governor of Minnesota]] and 2024 Democratic vice-presidential nominee File:Melissa Peterman by Gage Skidmore.jpg|[[Melissa Peterman]] (B.F.A.) – actress, [[Reba (TV series)|''Reba'']] File:Julia Ann Sears c 1872.jpg|[[Julia Sears]] – academic and [[Suffrage|suffragist]] File:Glen Taylor 20171004.jpg|[[Glen Taylor]] (B.S., 1962) – business magnate File:Adam Thielen 2017.jpg|[[Adam Thielen]] (B.S., 2012) – American football wide receiver File:Malavath Poorna.jpg|[[Malavath Purna|Malavath Poorna]] – Indian mountaineer, youngest female to scale [[Mount Everest]] File:Theresa Greenfield (cropped).jpg|[[Theresa Greenfield]] (B.A., 1987) – 2020 [[United States Senate|U.S. Senate]] candidate File:David Backes Boston Bruins 2017.jpg|[[David Backes]] (B.S., 2014) – Olympic ice hockey forward File:Mohamed Aden Tiiceey - 2018 (cropped).png|[[Mohamed Aden Tiiceey]] (M.A., 2005) – former president, [[Himan and Heeb]] ==See also== {{Portal|United States}} * [[List of colleges and universities in Minnesota]] == Notes == {{Notelist}} == References == {{Reflist |{{cite book |last1=Lagerquist |first1=Michael |editor1-last=Spear |editor1-first=Joe |title=Minnesota State University - 150 Years: An Evolution of Education |date=2018 |publisher=The Free Press Media}} {{cite web|title=The first woman to head a public college in the United States |url=https://www.mnsu.edu/reslife/housing/halls/about_julia_sears.html|website=About Julia A.
